## Problem

## Requirements

- Initial design: one machine accepts event submissions from clients.
- Increased demand: traffic has expanded by several orders of magnitude, so the one-server choke point needs to be eliminated.
- New functionality: support top-K computations across incoming events, such as the most frequent event categories, clients, or resources.
- Interview timing: 45 minutes, following a 10-minute behavioral introduction.

_Scalable event ingestion and top-K processing pipeline_

![Scalable event ingestion and top-K pipeline](https://cgppcnnkwbfiieexbrea.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/question-images/diagrams/80a2b9ac3bf7e6749935951a790b9f4f.svg)

## Notes

### Common deep dives

- How exactly-once versus at-least-once delivery affects the accuracy of top-K results.
- How watermarks and delayed events are handled for windowed top-K calculations.
- Persisting past top-K snapshots to enable trend reporting.
- Managing hot keys, where one highly dominant event category may require partitioning within that key.

## Preparation

- Understand Flink or Spark Streaming window semantics well enough to describe tumbling and sliding windows in two sentences apiece.
- Review a standard streaming top-K reference covering the usual talking points for this pattern.

## Hints

<details>
<summary>Hint 1</summary>

Think about how to distribute the event ingestion load across multiple machines while still being able to compute global top-K aggregates.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 2</summary>

Use a consistent hashing or partitioning scheme to route events to specific workers, and then use a distributed counter (e.g., Count-Min Sketch or HyperLogLog) for approximate top-K tracking.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 3</summary>

The key trade-off is between accuracy and latency: approximate algorithms can handle high throughput but may have small errors, so decide if exact top-K is required and if so, use a merge step.

</details>
